edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De carne Christi, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Qui fidem resurrectionis, ante istos Sadducaeorum propinquos sine controversia moratam, student inquietare, ut eam spem negent etiam ad carnem pertinere, merito Christi quoque carnem quaestionibus distrahunt, tanquam aut nullam omnino, aut quoquo modo aliam praeter humanam; ne si humanam constiterit fuisse, praejudicatum sit adversus illos eam resurgere omni modo, quae in Christo resurrexit. Igitur unde illi destruunt carnis vota, inde nobis erunt praestruenda. Examinemus corporalem substantiam Domini: de spiritali enim certum est. Carnis quaeritur veritas, et qualitas ejus retractatur, an fuerit, et unde, et cujusmodi fuerit. Renuntiatio ejus, dabit legem nostrae resurrectioni. Marcion, ut carnem Christi negaret, negavit etiam nativitatem; aut ut nativitatem negaret, negavit et carnem: scilicet, ne invicem sibi testimonium redderent et responderent nativitas et caro; quia nec nativitas sine carne, nec caro sine nativitate. Quasi non eadem licentia haeretica et ipse potuisset, aut, admissa carne, nativitatem negare, ut Apelles discipulus, et postea desertor ipsius; aut et carnem et nativitatem confessus. aliter illas interpretari, ut condiscipulus et condesertor ejus Valentinus. Sed et qui carnem Christi putativam introduxit, aeque potuit nativitatem quoque phantasma confingere, ut et conceptus, et praegnatus, et partus virginis, et ipsius exinde infantis ordo, τὸ δοκεῖν haberentur: eosdem oculos, eosdem sensus fefellissent, quos carnis opinio elusit.
pass_a_gloss: Those who strive to disturb the faith of the resurrection, which was delayed without controversy before those relatives of the Sadducees, so that they may deny that this hope also pertains to the flesh, rightly tear apart the flesh of Christ with questions, as if it were either none at all, or in some way other than human; lest, if it is established that it was human, it be prejudged against them that it rose again in every way, which rose again in Christ. Therefore, from where they destroy the vows of the flesh, from there we will have to rebuild them. Let us examine the bodily substance of the Lord: for the spiritual substance is certain. The truth of the flesh is sought, and its quality is retraced, whether it was, and from where, and of what kind it was. The announcement of it will give the law to our resurrection. Marcion, in order to deny the flesh of Christ, also denied the birth; or, in order to deny the birth, denied the flesh: clearly, so that birth and flesh might not give each other mutual testimony and respond to each other; because neither is birth without flesh, nor flesh without birth. As if the same heretical license had not also been possible for him, either to deny the birth, having admitted the flesh, like Apelles, his disciple and later deserter; or, having confessed both flesh and birth, to interpret them otherwise, like Valentinus, his fellow disciple and fellow deserter. But also, one who introduced the supposed flesh of Christ could equally have fabricated the birth as a phantom, so that the conception, and the pregnant virgin, and the birth, and the order of the infant from then on, might have been considered as appearances: they would have deceived the same eyes, the same senses, which the opinion of the flesh deceived.
pass_b_english: People who try to unsettle the faith of the resurrection — which those Sadducean relatives left undisturbed without controversy — so that they may deny that this hope also applies to the flesh, rightly tear Christ's flesh apart with questions, as if it were either nonexistent or somehow other than human; lest, if it is established as human, it be prejudged against them that it rose again in every way, since it rose in Christ. Therefore, from the very source where they destroy the promises of the flesh, we must rebuild them. Let us examine the Lord's bodily substance, for the spiritual substance is certain. The truth of the flesh is sought, and its quality is traced — whether it existed, where it came from, and what kind it was. Its declaration will give the law to our resurrection. Marcion, in order to deny Christ's flesh, also denied the birth; or, to deny the birth, he denied the flesh — clearly so that birth and flesh might not bear mutual witness and answer each other, because neither birth exists without flesh nor flesh without birth. As if the same heretical license were not also available to him: either to deny the birth while admitting the flesh, like his disciple and later deserter Apelles; or to confess both flesh and birth but interpret them differently, like his fellow disciple and fellow deserter Valentinus. But the one who introduced the supposed flesh of Christ could equally have fabricated the birth as a phantom, so that the conception, the pregnant virgin, the birth, and the subsequent order of the infant might have been mere appearances — deceiving the same eyes and senses that the opinion of flesh deceived.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. The translation of 'vota' as 'vows' (A) and 'promises' (B) is acceptable in this context of theological commitments/provisions. The Greek 'τὸ δοκεῖν' is correctly rendered as 'appearances' in Pass B. All clauses, including the complex conditional and the list of Christological stages, are preserved.

The Latin text is correctly identified as Tertullian's 'On the Flesh of Christ 1' from the Migne edition. The translation accurately reflects the source text, preserving all arguments, quotations, and doctrinal distinctions. The title 'The Reality of Christ's Flesh' appropriately names the thought of the passage. No OCR damage or uncertain readings are noted in the source.
